newsitem.title: USA: Lack of moisture stressing Midwest U.S. corn crop.
newsitem.headline: Lack of moisture stressing Midwest U.S. corn crop.

text.p: Below-normal rainfall during July is taking a visible toll on crops in Illinois, Missouri and Indiana and permanent yield losses are expected, agronomists said.
"I can't believe that we haven't lost a fairly substantial portion of the corn yield," said William Wiebold, agronomist at the University of Missouri in Columbia.
In central Missouri it has been so hot and dry that leaves on some corn plants are showing severe tissue damage, Wiebold said.
"The leaves are rolled and are actually sunburned," he said. "The tissue is actually turning gray and has been damaged because it has been so hot and dry."
Yield losses were certain because two weeks ago, when corn was in the critical pollination stage, temperatures climbed into the 90s and, in some ares, approached 100 degrees Fahrenheit, Wiebold said.
When corn pollinates under moisture and heat stress, the plant typically produces smaller ears and yields are lower, agronomists said.
In Illinois, which is usually the second largest corn producer in the United States, signs of moisture stress in the central part of the state are causing concern.
"I think there's not a question that the corn and bean crops are in a condition that would not be described as ideal," said Gary Pepper, agronomist with the University of Illinois in Champaign.

In areas where soil is sandier and holds less water, corn plants have rolled up their leaves in response to the hot weather and are unable to unroll them even in the cooler nighttime, said Dale Baird, a university extension agronomist in Peru, Ill.
"It's going to be a dry year and yields are going to be down," Baird said. "In a couple weeks we'll have a better sense of how pollination occurred."

Corn crops in the central part of Indiana spanning from Lafayette to Terre Haute are also begining to show signs of moisture stress and yields will likely be reduced, said Don Griffth, agronomist with Purdue University in West Lafayette.
"Most of this area has received less than an inch of rain during July," Griffth said. "The corn is not just stressing in the afternoon, it's stressing all day."
Griffth estimated that 10 to 15 percent of Indiana's corn crop was affected by overly dry conditions.

Forecasts for this weekend do not show much relief. Showers are expected to remain far north of the dry areas, and meteorolgists see no chance for significant rainfall until the middle of or late next week.
